title: Critical Velocity in Fluid Dynamics
short_intro: Critical velocity in fluid dynamics refers to the threshold velocity below which the flow of a fluid through a pipe is streamline (laminar) and above which it becomes turbulent. In the context of orbital mechanics, it also represents the minimum horizontal velocity required to launch a satellite into a stable circular orbit close to the Earth's surface.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of streamline and turbulent flow, Reynolds number basics, expression for critical velocity using dimensional analysis, Stokes' law, and terminal velocity of a small sphere falling through a viscous fluid.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Advanced derivation of critical velocity using Navier-Stokes equation principles, exact dependence on coefficient of viscosity and density, Poiseuille's formula, boundary layer separation, and orbital critical velocity in gravitational fields.

prerequisites: Coefficient of viscosity and Stokes' law

concept_notes.heading: Streamline versus Turbulent Flow
bullets: In streamline (laminar) flow, every fluid particle passing a given point maintains the same velocity and path as preceding particles, and flow lines do not cross.

When fluid velocity exceeds a certain limit called the critical velocity (v<sub>c</sub>), the flow pattern becomes irregular and chaotic, characterized by eddies and cross-currents known as turbulent flow.
The transition from laminar to turbulent flow depends on fluid density, viscosity, tube diameter, and mean velocity.

concept_notes.heading: Reynolds Number and Flow Regimes
bullets: The dimensionless Reynolds number (R<sub>e</sub>) governs the regime of fluid flow: R<sub>e</sub> = (\rho v d)/(\eta), where \rho is density, v is velocity, d is pipe diameter, and \eta is dynamic viscosity.
For flow in a circular pipe, R<sub>e</sub> < 2000 corresponds strictly to steady laminar flow.
Flow transitions between R<sub>e</sub> values of 2000 and 3000, while R<sub>e</sub> > 3000 guarantees fully developed turbulent flow.

concept_notes.heading: Dimensional Analysis of Critical Velocity in Pipes
bullets: Applying dimensional analysis, critical velocity v<sub>c</sub> depends on coefficient of viscosity \eta, density \rho, and tube radius r.

Dimensional formula of critical velocity is [M<sup>0</sup> L<sup>1</sup> T<sup>-1</sup>], viscosity is [M<sup>1</sup> L<sup>-1</sup> T<sup>-1</sup>], density is [M<sup>1</sup> L<sup>-3</sup> T<sup>0</sup>], and radius is [M<sup>0</sup> L<sup>1</sup> T<sup>0</sup>].
Equating exponents yields the proportional relation v<sub>c</sub> \propto \eta / (\rho r).

concept_notes.heading: Terminal Velocity and Viscous Drag
bullets: When a spherical body falls through an infinite viscous medium, viscous drag increases with velocity until it balances the net downward gravitational force minus buoyant force.
The constant maximum velocity attained by the falling body is termed the terminal velocity, given by v<sub>t</sub> = 2r<sup>2</sup>(\rho - \sigma)g / (9\eta).
Terminal velocity represents a steady-state condition distinct from pipe critical velocity, though both involve fluid viscosity parameters.

derivations.title: Derivation of Critical Velocity via Dimensional Analysis
derivations.conditions: Incompressible fluid flowing through a smooth cylindrical pipe of radius r.
steps: Assume critical velocity v<sub>c</sub> depends on coefficient of viscosity \eta, fluid density \rho, and pipe radius r such that v<sub>c</sub> = k \eta<sup>x</sup> \rho<sup>y</sup> r<sup>z</sup>, where k is a dimensionless constant.

Substitute the dimensional formulas: [M<sup>0</sup> L<sup>1</sup> T<sup>-1</sup>] = [M<sup>1</sup> L<sup>-1</sup> T<sup>-1</sup>]<sup>x</sup> [M<sup>1</sup> L<sup>-3</sup> T<sup>0</sup>]<sup>y</sup> [M<sup>0</sup> L<sup>1</sup> T<sup>0</sup>]<sup>z</sup>.
Equate the exponents of M, L, and T on both sides: For M: x + y = 0; For L: -x - 3y + z = 1; For T: -x = -1.
Solve the simultaneous equations: x = 1, y = -1, z = -1.
Substitute back to get the formula: v<sub>c</sub> = k \eta / (\rho r).

derivations.title: Derivation of Terminal Velocity for a Spherical Body
derivations.conditions: Sphere of radius r and density \rho falling through a fluid of density \sigma and viscosity \eta under acceleration due to gravity g.
steps: Downward forces acting on the sphere include true weight W = (4/3)\pi r<sup>3</sup> \rho g.
Upward buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid F<sub>b</sub> = (4/3)\pi r<sup>3</sup> \sigma g.
Viscous drag force opposing motion is given by Stokes' law: F<sub>v</sub> = 6\pi \eta r v<sub>t</sub>.
At terminal velocity v<sub>t</sub>, net downward force equals viscous drag: (4/3)\pi r<sup>3</sup> (\rho - \sigma)g = 6\pi \eta r v<sub>t</sub>.
Rearrange the equation to isolate terminal velocity v<sub>t</sub>.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Reynolds' Dye Filament Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic of a glass water tank with a central nozzle injecting a colored dye stream into flowing water through a horizontal glass tube.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At low flow rates, the dye forms a straight, distinct line indicating laminar flow. As velocity increases past critical velocity, the line wavers and breaks into diffusion, indicating turbulent mixing.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual questions regarding the visualization of critical velocity and transition to turbulence.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Velocity Profile across Pipe Radius
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Parabolic velocity distribution curve for laminar flow versus a flattened, blunt velocity profile for turbulent flow across a pipe cross-section.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Laminar flow exhibits maximum velocity at the center and zero at the walls (parabolic). Turbulent flow shows a uniform core velocity with a steep gradient very close to the walls.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT multiple-choice questions comparing velocity profiles in different flow regimes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Drag Force vs Velocity for Falling Sphere
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A linear curve passing through the origin representing Stokes' drag force against velocity up to the threshold of turbulence.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Direct proportionality holds at low velocities (Stokes' regime), which breaks down when inertial forces become comparable to viscous forces.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to test the validity limits of Stokes' law and terminal velocity equations.

solved_numericals.question: Water at 20°C flows through a tube of radius 1 cm. If the coefficient of viscosity of water is 1.0 × 10<sup>-3</sup> Pa·s and density is 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>, find the maximum average velocity for steady laminar flow, assuming the critical Reynolds number is 2000.
solution_steps: Identify given values: r = 0.01 m, D = 2r = 0.02 m, \eta = 1.0 × 10<sup>-3</sup> Pa·s, \rho = 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>, R<sub>e</sub> = 2000.
Use the Reynolds number relation for critical velocity: v_c = (R_e \times \eta) / (\rho \times D).

solved_numericals.question: A small steel ball of radius 2 mm and density 7800 kg/m<sup>3</sup> falls through glycerin of density 1200 kg/m<sup>3</sup> and viscosity 0.85 Pa·s. Calculate its terminal velocity. (Take g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>)
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: r = 2 × 10<sup>-3</sup> m, \rho = 7800 kg/m<sup>3</sup>, \sigma = 1200 kg/m<sup>3</sup>, \eta = 0.85 Pa·s, g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
Apply the terminal velocity formula: v_t = 2 r<sup>2</sup> (\rho - \sigma) g / (9 \eta).

solved_numericals.question: Determine the critical velocity of a satellite orbiting the Earth in a circular path just above its surface. Given Earth's radius R = 6400 km and g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
solution_steps: Identify parameters: R = 6400 km = 6.4 × 10<sup>6</sup> m, g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
Use the orbital critical velocity formula: v_c = \sqrt{gR}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Fluids are assumed to be incompressible and Newtonian, meaning viscosity remains constant regardless of shear rate.
Pipe walls are assumed to be perfectly smooth; surface roughness significantly alters the critical Reynolds number threshold.
Stokes' law and derived terminal velocity formulas assume an infinite fluid medium, ignoring boundary wall effects from container sides.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Critical velocity is a fixed, universal constant for all fluids.
common_misconceptions.correct: Critical velocity depends on tube dimensions, fluid density, and viscosity, varying from system to system.
common_misconceptions.why: It is a threshold parameter determined by the dimensionless Reynolds number of the specific flow geometry rather than a material constant.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Turbulent flow instantly occurs everywhere in a pipe once critical velocity is exceeded.
common_misconceptions.correct: Transition begins near the walls or downstream disturbances and gradually develops into fully turbulent flow across the cross-section.
common_misconceptions.why: Boundary layer separation and localized eddy formation precede complete flow breakdown.

quick_revision: Critical velocity marks the upper limit of streamline flow and the onset of turbulence in fluid conduits.
Reynolds number (R_e = \rho v D / \eta) determines flow regimes: R_e < 2000 is laminar, R_e > 3000 is turbulent.
Critical Velocity in Pipe: v_c = \frac{R_e \eta}{\rho D}
